title: Making It Easier for People to Ask for Help
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece examines why so many workplaces still treat asking for help as a sign of weakness rather than good judgment, and what that costs teams over time. It argues that healthy, high-performing teams are marked not by how few people need help but by how comfortable everyone is requesting it. The article outlines how leaders can shift the culture, starting with modeling their own help-seeking and clarifying who team members should turn to for specific expertise. Its central insight is a reframe: leaders who cast help-seeking as a gift to the helper, rather than a burden, make people more willing to ask, because being asked for help is itself a form of recognition.
points: Treating help-seeking as incompetence drives people to hide struggles, fueling stress, burnout, and worse performance.
Teams where help-seeking is normalized see faster problem identification, more trust, and better decisions.
Leaders should visibly model asking for help themselves to make it safe for others to do the same.
Naming specific go-to people before assignments begin reinforces that seeking help is expected, not exceptional.
The most effective reframe treats help-seeking as a compliment to the helper's expertise, not a burden on them.
quotes: In far too many organizations and teams, asking for help is viewed as a weakness rather than a smart move.
In teams where people feel comfortable asking for help, expertise becomes a shared asset.
In many instances, people would rather fail than admit they need a lifeline.
The best leaders promote the view that asking for help is a sign of respect for those who willingly offer it.
Contrary to common wisdom, the highest-performing teams aren’t the ones with the fewest people who need help.
